variants.name: ASP.NET Core service method over EF Core SaveChanges
variants.idiom_name: controller action -> service method -> DbContext.SaveChanges (one implicit transaction)
variants.implementation_notes: The dominant realization: a controller or minimal-API endpoint passes a DTO to a service method, which loads and mutates tracked entities and calls SaveChanges/SaveChangesAsync once - EF wraps all statements of that call in a transaction and leaves the database untouched if any of them fails. The script stays a straight line (query, decide, mutate, save) with no explicit begin/commit; DbContext.Database.BeginTransaction / IDbContextTransaction is used only when a script mixes EF with raw ADO.NET commands or must pin an isolation level, and manual transactions are incompatible with EF's retrying execution strategies.
pitfalls: Two SaveChanges calls in one script are two transactions - move the second change into the same call or open an explicit transaction.
AutoTransactionBehavior.Never lets a multi-statement save run non-atomically and can leave partial changes committed.
DbContext is a per-request unit of work: capturing it in a singleton or reusing it across requests leaks tracked entities and corrupts transaction state.

variants.name: ADO.NET service method with SqlTransaction
variants.idiom_name: service method with connection.BeginTransaction()/SqlTransaction and explicit Commit
variants.implementation_notes: The pre-EF realization, still common in ADO.NET and Dapper code: the script opens a connection, begins an explicit SqlTransaction (or DbTransaction), attaches it to every command, commits at the end and rolls back in the catch path. Choose it for batch-style scripts, for statements that need a specific isolation level or savepoint behaviour, or when raw commands must share one transaction with EF Core - in the ORM case, DbContext.Database.UseTransaction/DbContextTransaction is the bridge.
pitfalls: Commands executed before BeginTransaction, or with the transaction not attached, silently run outside it.
A missing rollback in the catch path leaves the pooled connection with an open transaction for the next borrower.
ADO.NET scripts are string-SQL sites: use parameters, never concatenation, and keep validation in one place.
